title: Fixed the ERSPAN Cisco marker packet dissector
description:
Additional Cisco documentation hints at implicit packing conventions
for the packet structure.

Also, during an attempt to get meaningful data out of ERSPAN timetstamps,
it was clear that there were issues in unpacking the packet's structure
given the tail value 0xA5A5A5A5 could not be confirmed.

Crossing other documents and observing actual data acquired
from a running Cisco Nexus 9000 device configured with granularity 4
(-> HW ASIC timestamp in 0.1pps) allowed to figure out the missing information
(endianness, field offsets and size) to get fields that make sense
when comparing two packets :
- Incremental sequence
- Differentials in values for ERSPAN fields
  for ASIC timestamps matching the differentials in UTC timestamps
- Differential value properly matching the device setting
  for delay between marker packets (0.1s),
  further corroborated by Ethernet packet arrival times
- Tail value properly displayed

Further, some field names have been changed :
- To reflect more accurately on the nature of the information in the data
  ("Timestamp" as documented by Cisco is actually the "ASIC 48-bit timestamp",
   whose exact meaning will depend on granularity,
   and not a trivially usable value such as a UNIX timestamp
   given it rolls over quite frequently,
   thus justifying the need for the marker packet
   in the first place to compute an absolute measure of time)
- To reflect the actual meaning of the value
  (The so-called "UTC" fields actually are
   ahead of the "packet arrival time" by the exact value of "UTC Offset" seconds,
   meaning they are actually following the "TAI" standard).

notes.body: approved this merge request
assigned to @JaapKeuter
Of note, the observed data was taken from a Nexus device running NXOS 9.2(3).
the change will don't break some other capture ?

Bonjour !

I just confirmed operation with NXOS 10.2(1), which returns an empty ASIC 48-bit timestamp. But it parses other fields properly, down to the tail value.

Also as far as I understand it, it should not break decoding. With my fix, you can see it will now consume data in such a way that it will reach the proper "tail" / signature field, and return the value "0xA5A5A5A5", which is what should be expected as per the white paper here : https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/products/collateral/switches/nexus-9000-series-switches/white-paper-c11-733921.html#_Toc413144488.

I'm not agreeing with this name change. The field is only representing TAI when UTC offset is zero. Once the UTC offset is properly set (as stated, currently at 37) then this represents UTC. Also nowhere is mention of TAI, neither in the documentation, the filter field, the header field name.

Just a quick note again regarding behavior on NXOS 10 which I have now fully validated with the fix, and the calculation logic for UTC timestamps for ERSPAN tagged packets, for which there is little available documentation.
This should also serve as further proof the ERSPAN timestamping feature works, and that wireshark can be used to compute the timestamps properly.

The calculation logic fundamentally hasn't changed, you still need to calculate things as follows :
```
Tag packet UTC timestamp = Marker UTC timestamp + ((Tag packet ERSPAN header ASIC timestamp - Marker ASIC timestamp) * Conversion factor)
```

Conversion factor in the case I have observed for my environment running with granularity set at 4, is 10^-10 because the ASIC timestamp is in hundreds of picoseconds :
```
NXOS 9.2 :
1637738514.552002588 + ( 45470837722137 - 45470587217177 ) * 10^-10 = 1637738514.577053070
1637738514.552002588 + 0.025050482 = 1637738514.577053070

NXOS 9.3, 10 :
1637818409.986294067 + ( 195600789977969 - 0 ) * 10^-10 = 1637837970.065291882
1637818409.986294067 + 19560.07899779690000000000 = 1637837970.065291882
2021-11-25 14:33:29 + 05:26~ = 2021-11-25 19:59:30 

(in +0900 timezone)
```

The marker packets on newer versions of NXOS will simply keep on broadcasting the UTC timestamp at which the ASIC timestamp has rolled over (thus the 0 value), thus simplifying the calculations while retaining compatibility with previous versions, provided you stick to the above formula.
